prerequisites: basics of the finite element method
fundamental concepts such as conservation laws (mass, energy, momentum)
knowledge of simulation software, such as Abaqus

learning_outcomes.text: Model and solve non-linear problems using advanced numerical tools, identifying sources of non-linearity (geometric, material and boundary conditions) and developing suitable models for analysing mechanical behaviour under large deformations or extreme conditions.
Demonstrate notions of incremental methods for solving non-linear problems and explicit and implicit time integration schemes for dealing with quasi-static and dynamic problems.

Carry out complex numerical analyses corresponding to elasto-plastic behaviour, post-critical buckling of a thin structure or perforation problems, and interpret the results of these simulations to assess structural reliability or optimise a design.

Develop a critical understanding of numerical simulation tools, explaining the inner workings of FEM codes (such as Abaqus), demonstrating an in-depth mastery that goes beyond the basic use of software, enabling them to tackle with confidence industrial or academic problems requiring advanced numerical modelling in solid mechanics.

syllabus_topics: Introduction to the non-linear finite element method
Origins, evolution and future trends of the finite element method.
Sources of non-linearity: geometric, material, boundary conditions.
Mathematical conventions and tensors in mechanics.
Time integration: implicit and explicit schemes
Elasto-viscoplastic models and radial return algorithms.
Material properties, boundary conditions, mesh convergence
assessment_rules: The evaluation formula is (1.2*DS1 + 0.8*TP1)/2. The weighting implies DS1 is 60% and TP1 is 40% of the final grade.
